**1 conditional emergent tension** — the **3-way retention/obligation interaction** (GDPR ceiling on personal data; AI Act floor on AI logs; CRA availability tail on update artefacts — three different data flows with three different obligation directions, with potential overlap on a single data flow when CRA update logs or AI logs contain personal data). The pairwise readings (GDPR↔CRA, GDPR↔AI_Act, CRA↔AI_Act) each handle two of the three axes, but the *non-pairwise observation* is that a single data stream (e.g. update logs from a CRA-classified high-risk AI product) may need to satisfy all three axes simultaneously: (a) the CRA update-availability tail applies to the update-artefact portion of the log; (b) the AI Act ≥6-month log-retention floor applies to the AI-system log portion; (c) the GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) `necessary` boundary applies to the personal-data portion. The high-level SO codifies this as a **layering rule, not a contradiction**: (a) identify the data class on the single data flow (update artefact vs AI log vs personal data); (b) apply the corresponding obligation direction (CRA availability floor on update artefacts; AI Act minimum floor on AI logs; GDPR ceiling on personal data); (c) when regimes overlap on a single data flow, **separation architecture** (pseudonymisation, separate retention rules, separate storage paths) is the controlled hand-off. The tension is **conditional** (it engages only when a CRA update log or an AI log contains personal data, or when a single data flow crosses regime boundaries) and is **regulated** by the separation-architecture requirement. Phase 1C Doc 07 documents the 3-axis layering architecture; Phase 3 case generation must surface the separation-architecture requirement explicitly when the case company's data flows cross regime boundaries. **No SCOPE-DISJOINT baseline pairs** — the 3×3 matrix shows **Conditional** scope overlap in baseline (Y or N depending on whether the data flow contains personal data); the baseline is not scope-disjoint across all three pairs. **No CONTRADICTORY pairs on the retention duty itself** — the 2 CORRECTED pairs (GDPR ↔ CRA and GDPR ↔ AI_Act) were relabelled from CONTRADICTORY to their correct classifications, and the relabelling is preserved verbatim. The **data-class divergence** (personal data / update artefacts / AI logs) is the **legitimately diverse dimension**: each regulator targets a distinct data class with a distinct obligation direction (ceiling vs floor vs floor), and the operational convergence is on the **3-axis layering rule** (GDPR ceiling + AI Act floor + CRA availability tail) with explicit axis-segregated hand-offs and separation-architecture requirement where regimes overlap on a single data flow. The **CRA 10-year tail is on update artefacts and Annex II information, NOT on personal data** — this is the rare-but-honest distinction that prevents the retention duty from being conflated across data classes; the controller-side GDPR `necessary` boundary remains the operative ceiling on the personal-data portion. The **AI Act 6-month floor is a floor-within-ceiling**, not a standalone obligation — the GDPR `necessary` boundary is the cap, the AI Act 6-month floor is the floor, the provider chooses the actual retention within the [6 months, "necessary"] range based on the intended purpose. The **CRA ↔ AI Act pair is genuinely N in baseline** (different objects, different actors, different purposes); the two obligations sit on different data flows and do not interact unless the same data flow is both a CRA update artefact and an AI Act log (a narrow window). The high-level SO surfaces the common retention/archiving duty as the 3-axis layering rule; the per-reg data class, obligation direction, trigger, anchor, lifecycle stage, recipient, and evidence template are documented separately in the three sub-SOs and the per-recipient evidence packs.

The OJ does not resolve this conflict. - **NIS 2 ↔ CRA** (propagated tension, CRDA line 217): same structural conflict — CRA user opt-out vs. NIS 2 Art. 21(2)(b) entity-level all-hazards detection capability (mandatory). For an NSIE deploying CRA-regulated products, the user's opt-out from CRA product-level monitoring does not legally exempt the NSIE from NIS 2 mandatory detection. - **CRA ↔ DORA** (propagated tension, CRDA line 340): same structural conflict — CRA user opt-out vs. DORA Art. 8(1) entity-level continuous monitoring (mandatory). For a DORA entity deploying CRA-regulated products, the user's opt-out from CRA product-level monitoring does not legally exempt the DORA entity from DORA Art. 8(1) mandatory continuous monitoring. **Operational consequence.** The two regimes can stack on the layered monitoring architecture (entity-layer mandatory + product-layer with opt-out) — the controller / NSIE / DORA entity must maintain the mandatory monitoring on the entity layer regardless of the CRA opt-out at the product layer.
